tier_reason: First-party benchmark with public code (bench/run_bench.sh, bench/bench_cofetch.cpp, bench_cpr.cpp, bench_httplib.cpp, bench/results.csv) and stated compiler and flags (gcc 14 -O3 Release), but the host is described only as WSL2 with 20 logical cores and no CPU model, so it cannot reach A; no independent measurement exists.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: '+35% single-thread throughput over the fastest sync client, +31% with one event loop per core against equal-sized thread pools, +16% on sequential chains driven from a busy-poll loop'. bench/README.md (results dated 2026-07-10), one thread, 20,000 GETs: cofetch 18,240 req/s (busy poll) and 17,412 req/s (run()) vs cpp-httplib 12,889 and cpr 10,127 (1.35x run() and 1.42x busy poll over cpp-httplib, derived from page data); 20 threads: cofetch 166,646 req/s vs cpp-httplib 127,333 and cpr 122,122 (1.31x, derived from page data); 2,000-request chain: cofetch busy poll 14,804 req/s vs cpp-httplib 12,761 and cpr 10,209 (1.16x, derived from page data), but cofetch run() 11,116 and coroutine 10,547 are slower than cpp-httplib. With 10 ms injected RTT one cofetch thread (9,353 req/s) ties 100-thread pools (cpp-httplib 9,571, cpr 9,345) and is about 98x a single-threaded sync client (95 and 94 req/s); at 50 ms RTT cofetch 1,819 req/s vs 100-thread pools about 1,918 (cofetch about 5% slower, derived from page data) and sync clients 20 req/s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 14 -O3 (CMake Release build driven by bench/run_bench.sh), libcurl 8.14 (system libcurl, also used by cpr via CPR_USE_SYSTEM_CURL=ON), asio 1.38; cpr 1.11.2 and cpp-httplib v0.20.0 pinned via FetchContent in bench/CMakeLists.txt; Debian 13 on WSL2; nginx from bench/nginx.conf (4 workers, keep-alive, access log off) on the same host
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark with public code (bench/) but the CPU model is not stated, so tier C. The headline is asynchronous (100 requests in flight on one thread) against synchronous clients with one request in flight, so the single-thread win measures concurrency, not a faster HTTP client. In the 20-thread tier cofetch splits 100 in-flight requests over 20 loops (5 each) while the cpr and cpp-httplib pools keep only 20 in flight, so 'equal-sized thread pools' still gives cofetch 5x the concurrency; those runs last only 0.12-0.16 s. The README's 'wins every scenario' is contradicted by its own RTT rows: at 10 ms RTT one cofetch thread only ties 100-thread pools (cpp-httplib's pool is 2% faster) and at 50 ms RTT the pools are about 5% faster (derived from page data). In the sequential chain the README uses the busy-poll mode: in the default run() mode cofetch (11,116 req/s) and its coroutine form (10,547 req/s) are slower than cpp-httplib (12,761 req/s), and the page says so. Loopback to a local nginx sharing the WSL2 host, not a real network; run-to-run variance about +/-10% per the page. Compared to cpr both sit on libcurl. The page also reports an internal epoll baseline about 14% faster than cofetch on loopback. The numbers (2026-07-10) predate commit c1bd40f (2026-09-29), which fixed leaked in-flight easy handles at Client destruction, resolver descriptors ignored by socket_cb and multi-block header parsing, and added transfer-node recycling; none of these affect the IP-literal, redirect-free benchmark's correctness, but the published numbers are from older code. HTTP client, filed under http-servers-frameworks for lack of a client category.

notes: Numbers and the bench harness check out; the drivers are honest (keep-alive sessions for cpr and cpp-httplib, status checked on every response) and the README's +35/+31/+16% match the bench/README tables, but the gain is from async multiplexing versus one-request-per-thread sync clients, the 20-thread tier gives cofetch 5x the in-flight requests, and the RTT rows show 100-thread pools tie or beat it (about 5% faster at 50 ms). Category: cofetch is client-only; http-servers-frameworks (Boost.Beast is a client and server library) is acceptable, and event-loops-io is the plausible alternative since the measured win comes from the asio reactor; neither cpr nor cpp-httplib is a listed baseline. Small project (8 stars, 2 forks) but published as a vcpkg port; MIT, last commit 2026-09-29.

tier_reason: First-party micro-benchmark whose full source and build command (g++ -O2 -std=c++11) are printed in the README 'How fast is it?' section, but no CPU model, compiler version or Boost/TCLAP version is given, and the source is not checked in as a file (no bench.cxx at the repo root), so it cannot reach A; no independent measurement.

corrections.caveats: First-party micro-benchmark whose full source is printed in the README, but no CPU model, compiler version, Boost version or date is given, so it cannot reach tier A; the source exists only in the README (no bench.cxx at the repo root). Each iteration times building the parser object plus one parse of a 13-token line, about 9 microseconds per iteration for args, which is irrelevant for a CLI that parses once per process. The author says the command line was trimmed to what TCLAP could handle. The README percentage wording is loose: the stated '220% faster' than boost::program_options matches a time ratio of about 2.2x (about 122% higher throughput), and '65% faster' than TCLAP is about 62% by time ratio (derived from page data). Nothing compares against getopt. The Boost loop copies the argument vector like the others but then parses the original carguments and never calls po::notify, so it does slightly less than a full Boost.Program_options use; asserts are enabled (#undef NDEBUG) in all three loops. Numbers are undated and probably from an old Boost release. Boost.Program_options is not one of the category's listed baselines (Bison/Flex, ANTLR, Boost.Spirit, nom): args is a command-line argument parser filed under parser-generators-and-combinators for lack of a closer category. The author describes the library as feature-complete (bug fixes still merged).

notes: README numbers and the derived ratios (2.22x vs boost::program_options, 1.62x vs TCLAP) check out against the printed run output; the harness is symmetric (each loop builds the parser and parses once). Fixed baseline_in_list to false since Boost.Program_options is not in the category's baseline list. Category fit is loose (CLI argument parser, not a parser generator), but no wave-3 category fits better. MIT, 1.6k stars, 187 forks, last commit 2026-10-05, author calls it feature-complete.
